# Ānāpāna Saṁyutta (SN 54)

**ID:** SN 54
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Ānāpāna Saṁyutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Linked Discourses on Breath Meditation
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/sn54
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0305m.mul9.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ānāpāna Saṁyutta* (SN 54), translated as the "Linked Discourses on Breath Meditation," is the fifty-fourth section of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated within the *Mahāvagga* [Gethin 2001; Bodhi 2005; SuttaCentral]. The collection centers on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*), revered as the primary meditation practiced by the Buddha himself before and after his awakening, and characterized as a peaceful dwelling (*tathāgatavihāra*) that stills discursive thoughts and trembling of the body [Gethin 2001; Bodhi 2005; Wen 2011; SuttaCentral]. Whereas other discourses treat breath awareness in a simple four-step formula, the suttas of SN 54 systematically expand it into sixteen steps or facets arranged into four tetrads [Bodhi 2005]. These four tetrads correspond directly to the four establishments of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), which in turn sequentially arouse and fulfill the seven factors of awakening (*bojjhaṅga*) [Gethin 2001; Bodhi 2005; Wen 2011; SuttaCentral].

Individual discourses highlight various doctrinal themes and historical episodes. In the *Ekadhamma Sutta* (SN 54.1), the basic practice formula is laid out [Polak 2011; SuttaCentral]. The *Mahākappina Sutta* (SN 54.7) describes how developing the "concentration of mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānasati-samādhi*) results in complete bodily and mental stillness [Wen 2011; Anālayo 2019]. In the *Vesālī Sutta* (SN 54.9), mindfulness of breathing is introduced by the Buddha as a peaceful remedy after a group of monastics engaged in foulness meditation (*asubha*) developed excessive revulsion toward their bodies and committed suicide [Anālayo 2018; Radich 2007; Wen 2011]. Other discourses, such as the *Kaṅkheyya Sutta* (SN 54.12) and the *Paṭhamaānanda Sutta* (SN 54.13), explicate training in relation to abandoning the hindrances and sequentially cultivating the awakening factors [Anālayo 2019; Wen 2011].

Ten discourses in the collection have direct Chinese parallels in the *Saṁyukta-āgama* (SĀ 803–813, preserved in T 99) [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2017; Anālayo 2019]. SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus agree on these cross-collection links to the *Saṁyukta-āgama*; DharmaNexus additionally aligns segments with the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* and *Vinayavibhaṅga*, the Sanskrit *Śrāvakabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, and the *Arthaviniścayasūtra* [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. The suicide episode in SN 54.9 shares extensive text reuse with the monastic Vinayas, particularly the Pali *Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga* (Pārājika 3), as well as the Dharmaguptaka and Sarvāstivāda Vinayas [DharmaNexus; Anālayo 2019; Radich 2007]. Internally within the Pali Canon, DharmaNexus demonstrates dense textual reuse between SN 54 and the *Ānāpānasati Sutta* (MN 118), the *Bojjhaṅga Saṁyutta* (SN 46), the *Satipaṭṭhāna Saṁyutta* (SN 47), the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* (*Ānāpānassatikathā*), and the *Visuddhimagga* [DharmaNexus].
